You are an elite forecaster with a strong track record on prediction platforms, specializing in social-science experiments. You reason from base rates and reference classes first, then adjust for specifics. You know that message interventions in megastudies typically produce small attitudinal effects and near-zero behavioral ones, and that forecasters' most common error is predicting effects that are too large.

Reference points for calibration:
- In comparable megastudies, average effects of single text messages on 0-100 attitude
  sliders are small: |ATE| typically 0-3 points, most often under 1 point.
- Effects of a single message exposure on real effortful behavior are typically near zero;
  low-cost in-survey actions (like agreeing to share a post) can move somewhat more.
- Proximal outcomes (beliefs directly targeted by the message) move more than distal
  ones (policy support, behavior).
- U.S. climate attitudes are strongly polarized; many liberals are near the scale ceiling,
  so headroom is concentrated among conservatives and moderates.
- A few messages backfire on some outcomes; the average message does not.

A preregistered online experiment (part of a 63-country 'intervention tournament') tested short interventions to stimulate climate action. This is the U.S. arm: 8,253 U.S. adults recruited online, ~670 per intervention arm and ~670 in control. Between-subjects design: each participant was randomly assigned to ONE intervention (or a neutral control text), then immediately completed the outcome measures. Belief and policy outcomes are 0-100 sliders.

CONTROL condition: participants read a neutral literary excerpt (from Dickens' Great Expectations) of similar length, reproduced below.

### Control_page1
Please carefully read the following excerpt (you may be asked about it in the following pages).

### Control_distract
As soon as the great black velvet pall outside my little window was shot with grey, I got up and went downstairs; every board upon the way, and every crack in every board calling after me, "Stop thief!" and "Get up, Mrs. Joe!" In the pantry, which was far more abundantly supplied than usual, owing to the season, I was very much alarmed by a hare hanging up by the heels, whom I rather thought I caught, when my back was half turned, winking. I had no time for verification, no time for selection, no time for anything, for I had no time to spare. I stole some bread, some rind of cheese, about half a jar of mincemeat (which I tied up in my pocket-handkerchief with my last night’s slice), some brandy from a stone bottle (which I decanted into a glass bottle I had secretly used for making that intoxicating fluid, Spanish-liquorice-water, up in my room: diluting the stone bottle from a jug in the kitchen cupboard), a meat bone with very little on it, and a beautiful round compact pork pie. I was nearly going away without the pie, but I was tempted to mount upon a shelf, to look what it was that was put away so carefully in a covered earthenware dish in a corner, and I found it was the pie, and I took it in the hope that it was not intended for early use, and would not be missed for some time.

### sciConsensus_1
Did you know that 99% of expert climate scientists agree that the Earth is warming and climate change is happening, mainly because of human activity (for example, burning fossil fuels) ? 

 Sources:  Myers  et al  2021  Environ. Res. Lett., 

 NASA: https://climate.nasa.gov/scientific-consensus/, 

 Lynas et al 2021 Environ. Res. Lett., 

 Doran et al., 2009, EOS

OUTCOME MEASURES (all answered immediately post-treatment):

[belief] (predict ATE in points on the 0-100 slider scale)
Belief in climate change: mean of 4 accuracy ratings (0-100 sliders) of the statements 'Human activities are causing climate change', 'Climate change poses a serious threat to humanity', 'Taking action to fight climate change is necessary to avoid a global catastrophe', 'Climate change is a global emergency'.

[policy] (predict ATE in points on the 0-100 slider scale)
Climate policy support: mean of 9 agreement sliders (0-100), 'I support...' raising carbon taxes on fossil fuels; expanding public transportation; more EV charging stations; more wind/solar energy; airline carbon taxes; protecting forests/land; green jobs investment; clean-waterways laws; taxes on carbon-intense foods.

[share] (predict ATE in probability (proportion willing to share, 0-1 scale))
Willingness to share climate information on social media (yes/no): participants saw a short factual climate post (about cutting food-related emissions by eating less meat/dairy) and were asked 'Are you willing to share this information on your social media?'. Predict the ATE as a change in the proportion answering yes (the control-group proportion is roughly 0.5).

[wept] (predict ATE in pages completed on the 0-8 task scale)
Work for Environmental Protection Task (real effortful behavior): a voluntary, tedious number-identification task of up to 8 pages; each completed page triggers a real tree-planting donation. Participants can stop at any time. Outcome = number of pages completed (0-8; the control-group mean is roughly 5).

Task: for EACH outcome, predict the average treatment effect (ATE) of THIS intervention versus the pooled control group — intervention mean minus control mean — in the outcome's native units as specified above. Consider the mechanism of this specific message, its likely reception across the U.S. political spectrum, measurement reactivity, and how it compares to typical messages in such megastudies. Small and null effects are common; sign matters — give your best point estimate, not a hedge toward zero if you genuinely expect an effect.

{"predictions": {"belief": <float>, "policy": <float>, "share": <float>, "wept": <float>}, "rationale": "<2-4 sentences>"}

Translation to policy support and especially voluntary effortful behavior should be much weaker, while the low-cost sharing outcome may show a small positive shift."}

According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change ( IPCC ), we have already reached more than 1°C of warming .

 99% of coral reefs will die off worldwide

### Q1.1
Life in the United States 

 Chicago, Illinois 

 It is no coincidence that where you live has very broad effects on your life and wellbeing.

In terms of material wellbeing, where you live affects the job and investment opportunities you have, the affordability of your housing, the taxes you pay, as well as the general state of the economy.

### futureSelf_passage1
Our collective behavior in the next decades will determine the extent to which Earth’s temperature will change. If no changes are made, the average temperature can increase by up to 6.5°C (12°F) by the year 2100 (IPCC, 2022). This would be extremely dangerous as super hurricanes, gigantic wildfires, and extreme food and water shortages would become common place. 

 Over the past century, the average temperature on Earth has increased by about 1°C (1.8°F). Human behaviors like energy production from fossil fuels, excessive meat consumption, and car driving increase the concentrations of greenhouse gases in Earth’s atmosphere. Over 90% of the increase in the world's temperature is caused by human activity.

Please put yourself in the year 2030 - eight years from now. Take a few moments to imagine your life in that future. Imagine how you will look, where you will be, and who you are with. It will be clear whether the necessary change occurred fast enough to match the speed of the changing climate. As the Earth’s atmosphere continues to heat up, the effects of climate change will be more apparent: the “highest observed temperature” records will keep being updated, heatwaves and the draughts will become more common, species will continue to become extinct.

Our collective behavior in the next decades will determine the extent to which Earth’s temperature will change. If no changes are made, the average temperature can increase by up to 6.5°C (12°F) by the year 2100 (IPCC, 2022). This would be extremely dangerous as super hurricanes, gigantic wildfires, and extreme food and water shortages would become common place. 

 Over the past century, the average temperature on Earth has increased by about 1°C (1.8°F). Human behaviors like energy production from fossil fuels, excessive meat consumption, and car driving increase the concentrations of greenhouse gases in Earth’s atmosphere. Over 90% of the increase in the world's temperature is caused by human activity.

Climate change is happening much more quickly , and will have a much greater impact , than climate scientists previously thought, according to the latest report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC, 2022). If your anxiety about climate change is dominated by fears of starving polar bears, glaciers melting, and sea levels rising, you are barely scratching the surface of what terrors are possible, even within the lifetime of a young adult today. And yet the swelling seas — and the cities they will drown — have so dominated the picture of climate change/global warming that they have blinded us to other threats, many much closer at hand and much more catastrophic.

### negEmo_passage3
Indeed, climate change involves more frequent and intense extreme events like floods, droughts, and fires, that are already causing widespread losses and damages to nature and people.  

 Approximately 3.3 to 3.6 billion people are highly vulnerable to climate change. 

 Without a massive change to how billions of humans conduct their lives, many parts of the Earth will likely become  uninhabitable by the year 2100 .  

 You will be able to advance the page shortly.

### negEmo_cliThresh
In 2015, scientists and policy makers internationally, agreed to limit future warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit; in the Paris Agreement). 
 Crossing the 1.5°C threshold risks unleashing severe climate change effects on people, wildlife and ecosystems. 

 Before reading this, did you know what the 1.5°C climate threshold is?

### negEmo_passage4
According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change ( IPCC ), we have already reached more than 1°C of warming .  

 If greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise, we could exceed 1.5°C as early as 2026.

 That is only 4 years away. 

In fact, if emissions remain close to current levels, we will pass the 2°C threshold between 16 to 50 years from now. 

 Is that within your lifetime? 

 It is within mine. 

 You will be able to advance the page shortly.

### negEmo_passage5
“It’s okay, internationally, governments are working to reduce our carbon emissions so that we do not pass the 1.5°C threshold.” 

If this is what you’re saying to yourself, you are wrong . 

 If we continue with the current policies, we will likely hit more than 3.1-3.7 degrees of warming by 2100. Even if all pledges are enacted, we will still pass both the 1.5°C and 2.0°C thresholds by quite a bit!

 You will be able to advance the page shortly.

### negEmo_passage6

 Compared to 1.5°C of warming, 2°C of warming involves: 

 Extreme rainfall/hurricane events become 70% more likely  
 Droughts will be  twice as frequent and twice as long  
 Twice as many people will not have reliable access to water 
 420 million more people will be frequently exposed to extreme heat waves 
 99% of coral reefs will die off worldwide 

 These consequences are just a few examples of a long list (for more, click here ).

The list of consequences is vast and complicated. However, one thing is sure…

 There is no escape 

Escape from human-caused climate change is no longer possible (IPCC, 2022). Climate change is now affecting every continent, every region, every ocean on Earth, and every facet of the weather. 

 Time is running out . 

 The window of opportunity to act to mitigate climate change is closing fast . We should take action now to avoid the worst consequences.

You predict new results by placing them in the distribution of published and replicated effect sizes, correcting for publication bias.

Reference points for calibration:
- In comparable megastudies, average effects of single text messages on 0-100 attitude
  sliders are small: |ATE| typically 0-3 points, most often under 1 point.
- Effects of a single message exposure on real effortful behavior are typically near zero;
  low-cost in-survey actions (like agreeing to share a post) can move somewhat more.
- Proximal outcomes (beliefs directly targeted by the message) move more than distal
  ones (policy support, behavior).
- U.S. climate attitudes are strongly polarized; many liberals are near the scale ceiling,
  so headroom is concentrated among conservatives and moderates.
- A few messages backfire on some outcomes; the average message does not.

A preregistered online experiment (part of a 63-country 'intervention tournament') tested short interventions to stimulate climate action. This is the U.S. arm: 8,253 U.S. adults recruited online, ~670 per intervention arm and ~670 in control. Between-subjects design: each participant was randomly assigned to ONE intervention (or a neutral control text), then immediately completed the outcome measures. Belief and policy outcomes are 0-100 sliders.

CONTROL condition: participants read a neutral literary excerpt (from Dickens' Great Expectations) of similar length, reproduced below.

### Control_page1

### Control_distract
As soon as the great black velvet pall outside my little window was shot with grey, I got up and went downstairs; every board upon the way, and every crack in every board calling after me, "Stop thief!" and "Get up, Mrs. Joe!" In the pantry, which was far more abundantly supplied than usual, owing to the season, I was very much alarmed by a hare hanging up by the heels, whom I rather thought I caught, when my back was half turned, winking. I had no time for verification, no time for selection, no time for anything, for I had no time to spare. I stole some bread, some rind of cheese, about half a jar of mincemeat (which I tied up in my pocket-handkerchief with my last night’s slice), some brandy from a stone bottle (which I decanted into a glass bottle I had secretly used for making that intoxicating fluid, Spanish-liquorice-water, up in my room: diluting the stone bottle from a jug in the kitchen cupboard), a meat bone with very little on it, and a beautiful round compact pork pie. I was nearly going away without the pie, but I was tempted to mount upon a shelf, to look what it was that was put away so carefully in a covered earthenware dish in a corner, and I found it was the pie, and I took it in the hope that it was not intended for early use, and would not be missed for some time.

Climate scientists are certain: 

 There is  no doubt  that humans are the main driver of climate change. Human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean, and land.

Climate change is already affecting every region across the world. It has resulted in more frequent and intense extreme weather events, causing widespread harm and damage to people, wildlife and ecosystems.

Human systems are being pushed beyond their ability to cope and adapt.

### Q5: Temp / Geo
In June to July 2021, there was a record-breaking heat wave in North America. It impacted cities like Portland, Oregon, Seattle, Washington, and Vancouver. 

500 excess deaths and 180 wildfires were recorded in British Columbia alone.

The temperature of 121.28 °F / 49.6 °C was recorded in the village of Lytton in British Columbia. This was record breaking for Canada. A wildlife nearly destroyed the entire village of Lytton. 

Scientists are certain that this heatwave was nearly impossible without climate change.

### Q6: Temp / Geo
In 2017 Hurricane Harvey struck Texas, followed by Hurricane Irma in Florida just over two weeks later.
 Hurricane Harvey and Irma impacted many U.S. states and killed 232 people. They caused around $175 billion (USD) in damage.

Shortly after, Hurricane Maria struck and destroyed over a third of homes in Puerto Rico. Over 4,600 people are thought to have died because of this storm.

### 1.5 Threshold
In 2015 scientists and policy makers internationally agreed to limit global warming to 1.5°C / 2.7°F, in the Paris Agreement. 

Warming above 1.5°C / 2.7°F risks severe climate impacts to people, wildlife, and ecosystems.

If we take little to no climate change action, how long do you think we have before we will reach 1.5°C / 2.7°F of warming? (Please enter a number)

### futureSelf_passage1
Our collective behavior in the next decades will determine the extent to which Earth’s temperature will change. If no changes are made, the average temperature can increase by up to 6.5°C (12°F) by the year 2100 (IPCC, 2022). This would be extremely dangerous as super hurricanes, gigantic wildfires, and extreme food and water shortages would become common place. 

 Over the past century, the average temperature on Earth has increased by about 1°C (1.8°F). Human behaviors like energy production from fossil fuels, excessive meat consumption, and car driving increase the concentrations of greenhouse gases in Earth’s atmosphere. Over 90% of the increase in the world's temperature is caused by human activity.

It will be clear whether the necessary change occurred fast enough to match the speed of the changing climate. As the Earth’s atmosphere continues to heat up, the effects of climate change will be more apparent: the “highest observed temperature” records will keep being updated, heatwaves and the draughts will become more common, species will continue to become extinct.

You are an elite forecaster with a strong track record on prediction platforms, specializing in social-science experiments. You reason from base rates and reference classes first, then adjust for specifics. You know that message interventions in megastudies typically produce small attitudinal effects and near-zero behavioral ones, and that forecasters' most common error is predicting effects that are too large.

Reference points for calibration:
- In comparable megastudies, average effects of single text messages on 0-100 attitude
  sliders are small: |ATE| typically 0-3 points, most often under 1 point.
- Effects of a single message exposure on real effortful behavior are typically near zero;
  low-cost in-survey actions (like agreeing to share a post) can move somewhat more.
- Proximal outcomes (beliefs directly targeted by the message) move more than distal
  ones (policy support, behavior).
- U.S. climate attitudes are strongly polarized; many liberals are near the scale ceiling,
  so headroom is concentrated among conservatives and moderates.
- A few messages backfire on some outcomes; the average message does not.

A preregistered online experiment (part of a 63-country 'intervention tournament') tested short interventions to stimulate climate action. This is the U.S. arm: 8,253 U.S. adults recruited online, ~670 per intervention arm and ~670 in control. messages.content:
You are an elite forecaster with a strong track record on prediction platforms, specializing in social-science experiments. You reason from base rates and reference classes first, then adjust for specifics. You know that message interventions in megastudies typically produce small attitudinal effects and near-zero behavioral ones, and that forecasters' most common error is predicting effects that are too large.

Reference points for calibration:
- In comparable megastudies, average effects of single text messages on 0-100 attitude
  sliders are small: |ATE| typically 0-3 points, most often under 1 point.
- Effects of a single message exposure on real effortful behavior are typically near zero;
  low-cost in-survey actions (like agreeing to share a post) can move somewhat more.
- Proximal outcomes (beliefs directly targeted by the message) move more than distal
  ones (policy support, behavior).
- U.S. climate attitudes are strongly polarized; many liberals are near the scale ceiling,
  so headroom is concentrated among conservatives and moderates.
- A few messages backfire on some outcomes; the average message does not.

A preregistered online experiment (part of a 63-country 'intervention tournament') tested short interventions to stimulate climate action. This is the U.S. arm: 8,253 U.S. adults recruited online, ~670 per intervention arm and ~670 in control. Between-subjects design: each participant was randomly assigned to ONE intervention (or a neutral control text), then immediately completed the outcome measures. Belief and policy outcomes are 0-100 sliders.

CONTROL condition: participants read a neutral literary excerpt (from Dickens' Great Expectations) of similar length, reproduced below.

### Control_page1
Please carefully read the following excerpt (you may be asked about it in the following pages).

### Control_distract
As soon as the great black velvet pall outside my little window was shot with grey, I got up and went downstairs; every board upon the way, and every crack in every board calling after me, "Stop thief!" and "Get up, Mrs. Joe!" In the pantry, which was far more abundantly supplied than usual, owing to the season, I was very much alarmed by a hare hanging up by the heels, whom I rather thought I caught, when my back was half turned, winking. I had no time for verification, no time for selection, no time for anything, for I had no time to spare. I stole some bread, some rind of cheese, about half a jar of mincemeat (which I tied up in my pocket-handkerchief with my last night’s slice), some brandy from a stone bottle (which I decanted into a glass bottle I had secretly used for making that intoxicating fluid, Spanish-liquorice-water, up in my room: diluting the stone bottle from a jug in the kitchen cupboard), a meat bone with very little on it, and a beautiful round compact pork pie. I was nearly going away without the pie, but I was tempted to mount upon a shelf, to look what it was that was put away so carefully in a covered earthenware dish in a corner, and I found it was the pie, and I took it in the hope that it was not intended for early use, and would not be missed for some time. 

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### Control_time
Timing
[Response options: First Click | Last Click | Page Submit | Click Count]

INTERVENTION — "Collective Action": participants saw the following intervention material (question prompts shown inline are part of the intervention experience).

### collectiveA_graphic1
What comes to mind when you think about climate change?

Do you sometimes feel that it is just beyond your capability make an to impact?

 Well you're not alone... 

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphic2
Research shows that people differ in their beliefs about whether they, other people, and the world can change:

With some people tending to believe change is possible 

And others viewing things as static and unchanging

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphic3
And our beliefs about the possibility of change determine if we act to make that change a reality.

These beliefs affect our ability to learn challenging new skills

To restore bad relationships, 

and even to solve conflict. 

 For example: Children with behavioral problems became 40% less aggressive after learning about the potential for personalities to change

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphic4
But what about climate change?

Is change possible there?

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphic5
Actually, yes!

When it comes to climate change, there is a lot to hope for, and our actions can make a real difference. 

 A recent report indicated that we are still in a window of opportunity!

 Smith et al., 2019, Nature Communications 

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphic6
But we have to act now, which requires us to come together and demand systematic change. 

   You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphic7
Systematic change has already solved past climate issues.

The Montreal Protocol, signed in 1987, phased out use of ozone-depleting chemicals, which helped to heal the hole in the ozone layer.  

   You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphic8
And protests to prevent climate change can have an impact:

For example, Margaret Klein wanted to see her community take bigger steps to address climate change 

So she joined an activist group in her town that held small demonstrations

The town responded by declaring a "climate emergency" and passing requirements shifting to renewable energy

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphic9
Since then, this has sparked a world-wide movement to pressure governments to declare climate emergencies.

So far, over 2,000 national and local governments have declared climate emergencies and implemented policy changes, eliminating 2.5 billion tons of carbon emissions just from the UK alone. 

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphi10
In Central America, years of activism by indigenous groups and civil society organizations have succeeded in pushing a number of governments to adopt The Five Forests Initiative

The Five Forests Initiative will protect 10 million hectares of forests and degraded land inside those forests, which is key to curbing climate change as they sequester carbon dioxide that would otherwise heat up the planet. 

   You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphi11
In Asia, activism is also having a big impact:

Eunbin Kang co-founded the Youth Climate Emergency Action Group

Together, they took action to prevent Doosan Heavy Industries & Construction from building more coal plants across Asia

They were also instrumental in pressuring the Korean government to pass its Green New Deal, which would cut 12.29 million tons of greenhouse gases. 

   You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphi12
Similarly, locals from across the American Midwest launched a campaign of protests and educational events in major cities to shift their region away from its reliance on fossil fuel transportation and towards electric vehicles 

Their campaign has pressured the governors of Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Minnesota, and Wisconsin to build a new network for charging electric vehicles.  

   You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphi13
So remember - change is possible! 

All it takes is for us to believe in it , follow the examples of Margaret, Eunbin, indigenous communities, and of local Midwesterners, and work together to make that change real.  

You will be able to advance the page shortly

OUTCOME MEASURES (all answered immediately post-treatment):

[belief] (predict ATE in points on the 0-100 slider scale)
Belief in climate change: mean of 4 accuracy ratings (0-100 sliders) of the statements 'Human activities are causing climate change', 'Climate change poses a serious threat to humanity', 'Taking action to fight climate change is necessary to avoid a global catastrophe', 'Climate change is a global emergency'.

[policy] (predict ATE in points on the 0-100 slider scale)
Climate policy support: mean of 9 agreement sliders (0-100), 'I support...' raising carbon taxes on fossil fuels; expanding public transportation; more EV charging stations; more wind/solar energy; airline carbon taxes; protecting forests/land; green jobs investment; clean-waterways laws; taxes on carbon-intense foods.

[share] (predict ATE in probability (proportion willing to share, 0-1 scale))
Willingness to share climate information on social media (yes/no): participants saw a short factual climate post (about cutting food-related emissions by eating less meat/dairy) and were asked 'Are you willing to share this information on your social media?'. Predict the ATE as a change in the proportion answering yes (the control-group proportion is roughly 0.5).

[wept] (predict ATE in pages completed on the 0-8 task scale)
Work for Environmental Protection Task (real effortful behavior): a voluntary, tedious number-identification task of up to 8 pages; each completed page triggers a real tree-planting donation. Participants can stop at any time. Outcome = number of pages completed (0-8; the control-group mean is roughly 5).

Task: for EACH outcome, predict the average treatment effect (ATE) of THIS intervention versus the pooled control group — intervention mean minus control mean — in the outcome's native units as specified above. Consider the mechanism of this specific message, its likely reception across the U.S. political spectrum, measurement reactivity, and how it compares to typical messages in such megastudies. Small and null effects are common; sign matters — give your best point estimate, not a hedge toward zero if you genuinely expect an effect.

Respond with ONLY a JSON object, no markdown fences, in exactly this form:
{"predictions": {"belief": <float>, "policy": <float>, "share": <float>, "wept": <float>}, "rationale": "<2-4 sentences>"}

You are an elite forecaster with a strong track record on prediction platforms, specializing in social-science experiments. You reason from base rates and reference classes first, then adjust for specifics. You know that message interventions in megastudies typically produce small attitudinal effects and near-zero behavioral ones, and that forecasters' most common error is predicting effects that are too large.

Reference points for calibration:
- In comparable megastudies, average effects of single text messages on 0-100 attitude
  sliders are small: |ATE| typically 0-3 points, most often under 1 point.
- Effects of a single message exposure on real effortful behavior are typically near zero;
  low-cost in-survey actions (like agreeing to share a post) can move somewhat more.
- Proximal outcomes (beliefs directly targeted by the message) move more than distal
  ones (policy support, behavior).
- U.S. climate attitudes are strongly polarized; many liberals are near the scale ceiling,
  so headroom is concentrated among conservatives and moderates.
- A few messages backfire on some outcomes; the average message does not.

A preregistered online experiment (part of a 63-country 'intervention tournament') tested short interventions to stimulate climate action. This is the U.S. arm: 8,253 U.S. adults recruited online, ~670 per intervention arm and ~670 in control. Between-subjects design: each participant was randomly assigned to ONE intervention (or a neutral control text), then immediately completed the outcome measures. Belief and policy outcomes are 0-100 sliders.

CONTROL condition: participants read a neutral literary excerpt (from Dickens' Great Expectations) of similar length, reproduced below.

In the pantry, which was far more abundantly supplied than usual, owing to the season, I was very much alarmed by a hare hanging up by the heels, whom I rather thought I caught, when my back was half turned, winking. I had no time for verification, no time for selection, no time for anything, for I had no time to spare. I stole some bread, some rind of cheese, about half a jar of mincemeat (which I tied up in my pocket-handkerchief with my last night’s slice), some brandy from a stone bottle (which I decanted into a glass bottle I had secretly used for making that intoxicating fluid, Spanish-liquorice-water, up in my room: diluting the stone bottle from a jug in the kitchen cupboard), a meat bone with very little on it, and a beautiful round compact pork pie. I was nearly going away without the pie, but I was tempted to mount upon a shelf, to look what it was that was put away so carefully in a covered earthenware dish in a corner, and I found it was the pie, and I took it in the hope that it was not intended for early use, and would not be missed for some time.

You are an elite forecaster with a strong track record on prediction platforms, specializing in social-science experiments. You reason from base rates and reference classes first, then adjust for specifics. You know that message interventions in megastudies typically produce small attitudinal effects and near-zero behavioral ones, and that forecasters' most common error is predicting effects that are too large.

Reference points for calibration:
- In comparable megastudies, average effects of single text messages on 0-100 attitude
  sliders are small: |ATE| typically 0-3 points, most often under 1 point.
- Effects of a single message exposure on real effortful behavior are typically near zero;
  low-cost in-survey actions (like agreeing to share a post) can move somewhat more.
- Proximal outcomes (beliefs directly targeted by the message) move more than distal
  ones (policy support, behavior).
- U.S. climate attitudes are strongly polarized; many liberals are near the scale ceiling,
  so headroom is concentrated among conservatives and moderates.
- A few messages backfire on some outcomes; the average message does not.

A preregistered online experiment (part of a 63-country 'intervention tournament') tested short interventions to stimulate climate action. This is the U.S. arm: 8,253 U.S. adults recruited online, ~670 per intervention arm and ~670 in control. Between-subjects design: each participant was randomly assigned to ONE intervention (or a neutral control text), then immediately completed the outcome measures. Belief and policy outcomes are 0-100 sliders.

CONTROL condition: participants read a neutral literary excerpt (from Dickens' Great Expectations) of similar length, reproduced below.

### Control_page1
Please carefully read the following excerpt (you may be asked about it in the following pages).

### Control_distract
As soon as the great black velvet pall outside my little window was shot with grey, I got up and went downstairs; every board upon the way, and every crack in every board calling after me, "Stop thief!" and "Get up, Mrs. Joe!" In the pantry, which was far more abundantly supplied than usual, owing to the season, I was very much alarmed by a hare hanging up by the heels, whom I rather thought I caught, when my back was half turned, winking. I had no time for verification, no time for selection, no time for anything, for I had no time to spare. I stole some bread, some rind of cheese, about half a jar of mincemeat (which I tied up in my pocket-handkerchief with my last night’s slice), some brandy from a stone bottle (which I decanted into a glass bottle I had secretly used for making that intoxicating fluid, Spanish-liquorice-water, up in my room: diluting the stone bottle from a jug in the kitchen cupboard), a meat bone with very little on it, and a beautiful round compact pork pie. I was nearly going away without the pie, but I was tempted to mount upon a shelf, to look what it was that was put away so carefully in a covered earthenware dish in a corner, and I found it was the pie, and I took it in the hope that it was not intended for early use, and would not be missed for some time. 

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### Control_time
Timing
[Response options: First Click | Last Click | Page Submit | Click Count]

INTERVENTION — "Collective Action": participants saw the following intervention material (question prompts shown inline are part of the intervention experience).

### collectiveA_graphic1
What comes to mind when you think about climate change?

Do you sometimes feel that it is just beyond your capability make an to impact?

 Well you're not alone... 

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphic2
Research shows that people differ in their beliefs about whether they, other people, and the world can change:

With some people tending to believe change is possible 

And others viewing things as static and unchanging

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphic3
And our beliefs about the possibility of change determine if we act to make that change a reality.

These beliefs affect our ability to learn challenging new skills

To restore bad relationships, 

and even to solve conflict. 

 For example: Children with behavioral problems became 40% less aggressive after learning about the potential for personalities to change

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphic4
But what about climate change?

Is change possible there?

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphic5
Actually, yes!

When it comes to climate change, there is a lot to hope for, and our actions can make a real difference. 

 A recent report indicated that we are still in a window of opportunity!

 Smith et al., 2019, Nature Communications 

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphic6
But we have to act now, which requires us to come together and demand systematic change. 

   You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphic7
Systematic change has already solved past climate issues.

The Montreal Protocol, signed in 1987, phased out use of ozone-depleting chemicals, which helped to heal the hole in the ozone layer.  

   You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphic8
And protests to prevent climate change can have an impact:

For example, Margaret Klein wanted to see her community take bigger steps to address climate change 

So she joined an activist group in her town that held small demonstrations

The town responded by declaring a "climate emergency" and passing requirements shifting to renewable energy

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphic9
Since then, this has sparked a world-wide movement to pressure governments to declare climate emergencies.

So far, over 2,000 national and local governments have declared climate emergencies and implemented policy changes, eliminating 2.5 billion tons of carbon emissions just from the UK alone. 

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphi10
In Central America, years of activism by indigenous groups and civil society organizations have succeeded in pushing a number of governments to adopt The Five Forests Initiative

The Five Forests Initiative will protect 10 million hectares of forests and degraded land inside those forests, which is key to curbing climate change as they sequester carbon dioxide that would otherwise heat up the planet. 

   You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphi11
In Asia, activism is also having a big impact:

Eunbin Kang co-founded the Youth Climate Emergency Action Group

Together, they took action to prevent Doosan Heavy Industries & Construction from building more coal plants across Asia

They were also instrumental in pressuring the Korean government to pass its Green New Deal, which would cut 12.29 million tons of greenhouse gases. 

   You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphi12
Similarly, locals from across the American Midwest launched a campaign of protests and educational events in major cities to shift their region away from its reliance on fossil fuel transportation and towards electric vehicles 

Their campaign has pressured the governors of Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Minnesota, and Wisconsin to build a new network for charging electric vehicles.  

   You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphi13
So remember - change is possible! 

All it takes is for us to believe in it , follow the examples of Margaret, Eunbin, indigenous communities, and of local Midwesterners, and work together to make that change real.  

You will be able to advance the page shortly

OUTCOME MEASURES (all answered immediately post-treatment):

[wept] (predict ATE in pages completed on the 0-8 task scale)
Work for Environmental Protection Task (real effortful behavior): a voluntary, tedious number-identification task of up to 8 pages; each completed page triggers a real tree-planting donation. Participants can stop at any time. Outcome = number of pages completed (0-8; the control-group mean is roughly 5).

[policy] (predict ATE in points on the 0-100 slider scale)
Climate policy support: mean of 9 agreement sliders (0-100), 'I support...' raising carbon taxes on fossil fuels; expanding public transportation; more EV charging stations; more wind/solar energy; airline carbon taxes; protecting forests/land; green jobs investment; clean-waterways laws; taxes on carbon-intense foods.

[belief] (predict ATE in points on the 0-100 slider scale)
Belief in climate change: mean of 4 accuracy ratings (0-100 sliders) of the statements 'Human activities are causing climate change', 'Climate change poses a serious threat to humanity', 'Taking action to fight climate change is necessary to avoid a global catastrophe', 'Climate change is a global emergency'.

[share] (predict ATE in probability (proportion willing to share, 0-1 scale))
Willingness to share climate information on social media (yes/no): participants saw a short factual climate post (about cutting food-related emissions by eating less meat/dairy) and were asked 'Are you willing to share this information on your social media?'. Predict the ATE as a change in the proportion answering yes (the control-group proportion is roughly 0.5).

Task: for EACH outcome, predict the average treatment effect (ATE) of THIS intervention versus the pooled control group — intervention mean minus control mean — in the outcome's native units as specified above. Consider the mechanism of this specific message, its likely reception across the U.S. political spectrum, measurement reactivity, and how it compares to typical messages in such megastudies. Small and null effects are common; sign matters — give your best point estimate, not a hedge toward zero if you genuinely expect an effect.

Respond with ONLY a JSON object, no markdown fences, in exactly this form:
{"predictions": {"wept": <float>, "policy": <float>, "belief": <float>, "share": <float>}, "rationale": "<2-4 sentences>"}

You reason from base rates and reference classes first, then adjust for specifics. You know that message interventions in megastudies typically produce small attitudinal effects and near-zero behavioral ones, and that forecasters' most common error is predicting effects that are too large.

Reference points for calibration:
- In comparable megastudies, average effects of single text messages on 0-100 attitude
  sliders are small: |ATE| typically 0-3 points, most often under 1 point.
- Effects of a single message exposure on real effortful behavior are typically near zero;
  low-cost in-survey actions (like agreeing to share a post) can move somewhat more.
- Proximal outcomes (beliefs directly targeted by the message) move more than distal
  ones (policy support, behavior).
- U.S. climate attitudes are strongly polarized; many liberals are near the scale ceiling,
  so headroom is concentrated among conservatives and moderates.
- A few messages backfire on some outcomes; the average message does not.

A preregistered online experiment (part of a 63-country 'intervention tournament') tested short interventions to stimulate climate action. This is the U.S. arm: 8,253 U.S. adults recruited online, ~670 per intervention arm and ~670 in control. Between-subjects design: each participant was randomly assigned to ONE intervention (or a neutral control text), then immediately completed the outcome measures. ### Control_distract

In the pantry, which was far more abundantly supplied than usual, owing to the season, I was very much alarmed by a hare hanging up by the heels, whom I rather thought I caught, when my back was half turned, winking. I had no time for verification, no time for selection, no time for anything, for I had no time to spare. I stole some bread, some rind of cheese, about half a jar of mincemeat (which I tied up in my pocket-handkerchief with my last night’s slice), some brandy from a stone bottle (which I decanted into a glass bottle I had secretly used for making that intoxicating fluid, Spanish-liquorice-water, up in my room: diluting the stone bottle from a jug in the kitchen cupboard), a meat bone with very little on it, and a beautiful round compact pork pie. You know that message interventions in megastudies typically produce small attitudinal effects and near-zero behavioral ones, and that forecasters' most common error is predicting effects that are too large.

A preregistered online experiment (part of a 63-country 'intervention tournament') tested short interventions to stimulate climate action. This is the U.S. arm: 8,253 U.S. adults recruited online, ~670 per intervention arm and ~670 in control. Between-subjects design: each participant was randomly assigned to ONE intervention (or a neutral control text), then immediately completed the outcome measures. Belief and policy outcomes are 0-100 sliders.

CONTROL condition: participants read a neutral literary excerpt (from Dickens' Great Expectations) of similar length, reproduced below.

### Control_page1
Please carefully read the following excerpt (you may be asked about it in the following pages).

### Control_distract
As soon as the great black velvet pall outside my little window was shot with grey, I got up and went downstairs; every board upon the way, and every crack in every board calling after me, "Stop thief!" and "Get up, Mrs. Joe!" In the pantry, which was far more abundantly supplied than usual, owing to the season, I was very much alarmed by a hare hanging up by the heels, whom I rather thought I caught, when my back was half turned, winking. I had no time for verification, no time for selection, no time for anything, for I had no time to spare. I stole some bread, some rind of cheese, about half a jar of mincemeat (which I tied up in my pocket-handkerchief with my last night’s slice), some brandy from a stone bottle (which I decanted into a glass bottle I had secretly used for making that intoxicating fluid, Spanish-liquorice-water, up in my room: diluting the stone bottle from a jug in the kitchen cupboard), a meat bone with very little on it, and a beautiful round compact pork pie. I was nearly going away without the pie, but I was tempted to mount upon a shelf, to look what it was that was put away so carefully in a covered earthenware dish in a corner, and I found it was the pie, and I took it in the hope that it was not intended for early use, and would not be missed for some time. 

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### Control_time
Timing
[Response options: First Click | Last Click | Page Submit | Click Count]

INTERVENTION — "Working Together Norm": participants saw the following intervention material (question prompts shown inline are part of the intervention experience).

### identity_intro
In what follows, you will be shown a flyer and then you will be asked to answer a series of questions. 
 The flyer will be on the screen for 20 seconds, during which you are encouraged to read the information it displays. After 20 seconds you will be able to advance the page.

### identity_intro2
Imagine you are seeing this flyer in your neighborhood. Please read it carefully!  
 You will be able to advance the page in 20 seconds.

### identity_scale1
If you are taking steps towards reducing your carbon footprint, to what extent would you feel like
you are doing so together with other Americans?

### identity_scale2
To what extent do you feel like taking steps towards reducing your carbon footprint is something shared with other Americans?

### Identity_scale3
To what extent do you feel like taking steps towards reducing your carbon footprint involves a sense of togetherness with other Americans?

### identity_scale4
How common do you think it is for Americans to take steps towards reducing their carbon footprint?

### identity_scale5
How often do you think Americans make an effort towards reducing their carbon footprint?

### identity_scale6
How many Americans do you think make an effort towards reducing their carbon footprint?

### identity_scale7
How much do you
feel like other Americans think it is good to take steps towards reducing their carbon footprint?

### identity_scale8
How much do you
feel like other Americans think you should take steps towards reducing your carbon footprint?

### identity_scale9
How strongly do you identify with your fellow Americans?

### identity_scale10
How important is being American to your identity?

### identity_scale11
How important is being similar to other Americans to you?

### identity_scale12
How interested are you in reducing your carbon emissions?

### identity_scale13
To what degree do you support policies aimed at reducing greenhouse gasses?

### identity_scale14
To what degree would you share climate change information on social media?

### identity_scale15
How interested are you in donating to tree planting organizations?

OUTCOME MEASURES (all answered immediately post-treatment):

[wept] (predict ATE in pages completed on the 0-8 task scale)
Work for Environmental Protection Task (real effortful behavior): a voluntary, tedious number-identification task of up to 8 pages; each completed page triggers a real tree-planting donation. Participants can stop at any time. Outcome = number of pages completed (0-8; the control-group mean is roughly 5).

[policy] (predict ATE in points on the 0-100 slider scale)
Climate policy support: mean of 9 agreement sliders (0-100), 'I support...' raising carbon taxes on fossil fuels; expanding public transportation; more EV charging stations; more wind/solar energy; airline carbon taxes; protecting forests/land; green jobs investment; clean-waterways laws; taxes on carbon-intense foods.

[belief] (predict ATE in points on the 0-100 slider scale)
Belief in climate change: mean of 4 accuracy ratings (0-100 sliders) of the statements 'Human activities are causing climate change', 'Climate change poses a serious threat to humanity', 'Taking action to fight climate change is necessary to avoid a global catastrophe', 'Climate change is a global emergency'.

[share] (predict ATE in probability (proportion willing to share, 0-1 scale))
Willingness to share climate information on social media (yes/no): participants saw a short factual climate post (about cutting food-related emissions by eating less meat/dairy) and were asked 'Are you willing to share this information on your social media?'. Predict the ATE as a change in the proportion answering yes (the control-group proportion is roughly 0.5).

Reference points for calibration:
- In comparable megastudies, average effects of single text messages on 0-100 attitude
  sliders are small: |ATE| typically 0-3 points, most often under 1 point.
- Effects of a single message exposure on real effortful behavior are typically near zero;
  low-cost in-survey actions (like agreeing to share a post) can move somewhat more.
- Proximal outcomes (beliefs directly targeted by the message) move more than distal
  ones (policy support, behavior).
- U.S. climate attitudes are strongly polarized; many liberals are near the scale ceiling,
  so headroom is concentrated among conservatives and moderates.
- A few messages backfire on some outcomes; the average message does not.

Task: for EACH outcome, predict the average treatment effect (ATE) of THIS intervention versus the pooled control group — intervention mean minus control mean — in the outcome's native units as specified above. Consider the mechanism of this specific message, its likely reception across the U.S. political spectrum, measurement reactivity, and how it compares to typical messages in such megastudies. Small and null effects are common; sign matters — give your best point estimate, not a hedge toward zero if you genuinely expect an effect.

Respond with ONLY a JSON object, no markdown fences, in exactly this form:
{"predictions": {"wept": <float>, "policy": <float>, "belief": <float>, "share": <float>}, "rationale": "<2-4 sentences>"}

messages.content: You are an elite forecaster with a strong track record on prediction platforms, specializing in social-science experiments. You reason from base rates and reference classes first, then adjust for specifics. You know that message interventions in megastudies typically produce small attitudinal effects and near-zero behavioral ones, and that forecasters' most common error is predicting effects that are too large.

A preregistered online experiment (part of a 63-country 'intervention tournament') tested short interventions to stimulate climate action. This is the U.S. arm: 8,253 U.S. adults recruited online, ~670 per intervention arm and ~670 in control. Between-subjects design: each participant was randomly assigned to ONE intervention (or a neutral control text), then immediately completed the outcome measures. Belief and policy outcomes are 0-100 sliders.

CONTROL condition: participants read a neutral literary excerpt (from Dickens' Great Expectations) of similar length, reproduced below.

### Control_page1
Please carefully read the following excerpt (you may be asked about it in the following pages).

### Control_distract
As soon as the great black velvet pall outside my little window was shot with grey, I got up and went downstairs; every board upon the way, and every crack in every board calling after me, "Stop thief!" and "Get up, Mrs. Joe!" In the pantry, which was far more abundantly supplied than usual, owing to the season, I was very much alarmed by a hare hanging up by the heels, whom I rather thought I caught, when my back was half turned, winking. I had no time for verification, no time for selection, no time for anything, for I had no time to spare. I stole some bread, some rind of cheese, about half a jar of mincemeat (which I tied up in my pocket-handkerchief with my last night’s slice), some brandy from a stone bottle (which I decanted into a glass bottle I had secretly used for making that intoxicating fluid, Spanish-liquorice-water, up in my room: diluting the stone bottle from a jug in the kitchen cupboard), a meat bone with very little on it, and a beautiful round compact pork pie. I was nearly going away without the pie, but I was tempted to mount upon a shelf, to look what it was that was put away so carefully in a covered earthenware dish in a corner, and I found it was the pie, and I took it in the hope that it was not intended for early use, and would not be missed for some time. 

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### Control_time
Timing
[Response options: First Click | Last Click | Page Submit | Click Count]

INTERVENTION — "Future Self-Continuity": participants saw the following intervention material (question prompts shown inline are part of the intervention experience).

### futureSelf_passage1
Our collective behavior in the next decades will determine the extent to which Earth’s temperature will change. If no changes are made, the average temperature can increase by up to 6.5°C (12°F) by the year 2100 (IPCC, 2022). This would be extremely dangerous as super hurricanes, gigantic wildfires, and extreme food and water shortages would become common place. 

 Over the past century, the average temperature on Earth has increased by about 1°C (1.8°F). Human behaviors like energy production from fossil fuels, excessive meat consumption, and car driving increase the concentrations of greenhouse gases in Earth’s atmosphere. Over 90% of the increase in the world's temperature is caused by human activity. 

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### futureSelf_instruct
Please put yourself in the year 2030 - eight years from now. Take a few moments to imagine your life in that future. Imagine how you will look, where you will be, and who you are with. In the year 2030, it will be clear whether keeping climate change under 2°C is still possible. It will be clear whether the necessary change occurred fast enough to match the speed of the changing climate. As the Earth’s atmosphere continues to heat up, the effects of climate change will be more apparent: the “highest observed temperature” records will keep being updated, heatwaves and the draughts will become more common, species will continue to become extinct.

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

### futureSelf_letter
Now please write yourself a “letter from the future”. This should be a letter you are writing in the year 2030, to your past self. As the person that you will be in 2030, what role would you think would be appropriate for you in respect to climate change? What would you want to tell yourself in the past? What would you like your past self to do?  

Please spend a bit of time on this task and try to write at least 100 words (5 sentences), or more, if possible.

 You will be able to advance the page after at least one minute has passed

### Q247
Thank you for your responses, we will now ask you some questions about your climate change perceptions.

OUTCOME MEASURES (all answered immediately post-treatment):

[wept] (predict ATE in pages completed on the 0-8 task scale)
Work for Environmental Protection Task (real effortful behavior): a voluntary, tedious number-identification task of up to 8 pages; each completed page triggers a real tree-planting donation. Participants can stop at any time. Outcome = number of pages completed (0-8; the control-group mean is roughly 5).

[policy] (predict ATE in points on the 0-100 slider scale)
Climate policy support: mean of 9 agreement sliders (0-100), 'I support...' raising carbon taxes on fossil fuels; expanding public transportation; more EV charging stations; more wind/solar energy; airline carbon taxes; protecting forests/land; green jobs investment; clean-waterways laws; taxes on carbon-intense foods.

[belief] (predict ATE in points on the 0-100 slider scale)
Belief in climate change: mean of 4 accuracy ratings (0-100 sliders) of the statements 'Human activities are causing climate change', 'Climate change poses a serious threat to humanity', 'Taking action to fight climate change is necessary to avoid a global catastrophe', 'Climate change is a global emergency'.

[share] (predict ATE in probability (proportion willing to share, 0-1 scale))
Willingness to share climate information on social media (yes/no): participants saw a short factual climate post (about cutting food-related emissions by eating less meat/dairy) and were asked 'Are you willing to share this information on your social media?'. Predict the ATE as a change in the proportion answering yes (the control-group proportion is roughly 0.5).

You are a quantitative social scientist who has run and reviewed dozens of preregistered field experiments on science communication. You think in terms of statistical power, measurement reactivity, ceiling effects, and the gap between attitudes and behavior. You are skeptical of large claimed effects.

Reference points for calibration:
- In comparable megastudies, average effects of single text messages on 0-100 attitude
  sliders are small: |ATE| typically 0-3 points, most often under 1 point.
- Effects of a single message exposure on real effortful behavior are typically near zero;
  low-cost in-survey actions (like agreeing to share a post) can move somewhat more.
- Proximal outcomes (beliefs directly targeted by the message) move more than distal
  ones (policy support, behavior).
- U.S. climate attitudes are strongly polarized; many liberals are near the scale ceiling,
  so headroom is concentrated among conservatives and moderates.
- A few messages backfire on some outcomes; the average message does not.

A preregistered online experiment (part of a 63-country 'intervention tournament') tested short interventions to stimulate climate action. This is the U.S. arm: 8,253 U.S. adults recruited online, ~670 per intervention arm and ~670 in control. Between-subjects design: each participant was randomly assigned to ONE intervention (or a neutral control text), then immediately completed the outcome measures. Belief and policy outcomes are 0-100 sliders.

You are a quantitative social scientist who has run and reviewed dozens of preregistered field experiments on science communication. You think in terms of statistical power, measurement reactivity, ceiling effects, and the gap between attitudes and behavior. You are skeptical of large claimed effects.

Reference points for calibration:
- In comparable megastudies, average effects of single text messages on 0-100 attitude
  sliders are small: |ATE| typically 0-3 points, most often under 1 point.
- Effects of a single message exposure on real effortful behavior are typically near zero;
  low-cost in-survey actions (like agreeing to share a post) can move somewhat more.
- Proximal outcomes (beliefs directly targeted by the message) move more than distal
  ones (policy support, behavior).
- U.S. climate attitudes are strongly polarized; many liberals are near the scale ceiling,
  so headroom is concentrated among conservatives and moderates.
- A few messages backfire on some outcomes; the average message does not.

A preregistered online experiment (part of a 63-country 'intervention tournament') tested short interventions to stimulate climate action. This is the U.S. arm: 8,253 U.S. adults recruited online, ~670 per intervention arm and ~670 in control. Between-subjects design: each participant was randomly assigned to ONE intervention (or a neutral control text), then immediately completed the outcome measures. Belief and policy outcomes are 0-100 sliders.

CONTROL condition: participants read a neutral literary excerpt (from Dickens' Great Expectations) of similar length, reproduced below.

### Control_page1

### Control_distract
As soon as the great black velvet pall outside my little window was shot with grey, I got up and went downstairs; every board upon the way, and every crack in every board calling after me, "Stop thief!" and "Get up, Mrs. Joe!" In the pantry, which was far more abundantly supplied than usual, owing to the season, I was very much alarmed by a hare hanging up by the heels, whom I rather thought I caught, when my back was half turned, winking. I had no time for verification, no time for selection, no time for anything, for I had no time to spare. I stole some bread, some rind of cheese, about half a jar of mincemeat (which I tied up in my pocket-handkerchief with my last night’s slice), some brandy from a stone bottle (which I decanted into a glass bottle I had secretly used for making that intoxicating fluid, Spanish-liquorice-water, up in my room: diluting the stone bottle from a jug in the kitchen cupboard), a meat bone with very little on it, and a beautiful round compact pork pie. I was nearly going away without the pie, but I was tempted to mount upon a shelf, to look what it was that was put away so carefully in a covered earthenware dish in a corner, and I found it was the pie, and I took it in the hope that it was not intended for early use, and would not be missed for some time.

To restore bad relationships,

 Smith et al., 2019, Nature Communications

Eunbin Kang co-founded the Youth Climate Emergency Action Group

Together, they took action to prevent Doosan Heavy Industries & Construction from building more coal plants across Asia

They were also instrumental in pressuring the Korean government to pass its Green New Deal, which would cut 12.29 million tons of greenhouse gases. 

   You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphi12
Similarly, locals from across the American Midwest launched a campaign of protests and educational events in major cities to shift their region away from its reliance on fossil fuel transportation and towards electric vehicles 

Their campaign has pressured the governors of Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Minnesota, and Wisconsin to build a new network for charging electric vehicles.  

   You will be able to advance the page shortly

### collectiveA_graphi13
So remember - change is possible! 

All it takes is for us to believe in it , follow the examples of Margaret, Eunbin, indigenous communities, and of local Midwesterners, and work together to make that change real.  

You will be able to advance the page shortly

You are a quantitative social scientist who has run and reviewed dozens of preregistered field experiments on science communication. You think in terms of statistical power, measurement reactivity, ceiling effects, and the gap between attitudes and behavior. You are skeptical of large claimed effects.

Reference points for calibration:
- In comparable megastudies, average effects of single text messages on 0-100 attitude
  sliders are small: |ATE| typically 0-3 points, most often under 1 point.
- Effects of a single message exposure on real effortful behavior are typically near zero;
  low-cost in-survey actions (like agreeing to share a post) can move somewhat more.
- Proximal outcomes (beliefs directly targeted by the message) move more than distal
  ones (policy support, behavior).
- U.S. climate attitudes are strongly polarized; many liberals are near the scale ceiling,
  so headroom is concentrated among conservatives and moderates.
- A few messages backfire on some outcomes; the average message does not.

A preregistered online experiment (part of a 63-country 'intervention tournament') tested short interventions to stimulate climate action. This is the U.S. arm: 8,253 U.S. adults recruited online, ~670 per intervention arm and ~670 in control. Between-subjects design: each participant was randomly assigned to ONE intervention (or a neutral control text), then immediately completed the outcome measures. Belief and policy outcomes are 0-100 sliders.

CONTROL condition: participants read a neutral literary excerpt (from Dickens' Great Expectations) of similar length, reproduced below.

### Control_page1
Please carefully read the following excerpt (you may be asked about it in the following pages).

### Control_distract
As soon as the great black velvet pall outside my little window was shot with grey, I got up and went downstairs; every board upon the way, and every crack in every board calling after me, "Stop thief!" and "Get up, Mrs. Joe!" In the pantry, which was far more abundantly supplied than usual, owing to the season, I was very much alarmed by a hare hanging up by the heels, whom I rather thought I caught, when my back was half turned, winking. I had no time for verification, no time for selection, no time for anything, for I had no time to spare. I stole some bread, some rind of cheese, about half a jar of mincemeat (which I tied up in my pocket-handkerchief with my last night’s slice), some brandy from a stone bottle (which I decanted into a glass bottle I had secretly used for making that intoxicating fluid, Spanish-liquorice-water, up in my room: diluting the stone bottle from a jug in the kitchen cupboard), a meat bone with very little on it, and a beautiful round compact pork pie. I was nearly going away without the pie, but I was tempted to mount upon a shelf, to look what it was that was put away so carefully in a covered earthenware dish in a corner, and I found it was the pie, and I took it in the hope that it was not intended for early use, and would not be missed for some time.

Climate policy support: mean of 9 agreement sliders (0-100), 'I support...' raising carbon taxes on fossil fuels; expanding public transportation; more EV charging stations; more wind/solar energy; airline carbon taxes; protecting forests/land; green jobs investment; clean-waterways laws; taxes on carbon-intense foods.

You are a quantitative social scientist who has run and reviewed dozens of preregistered field experiments on science communication. You think in terms of statistical power, measurement reactivity, ceiling effects, and the gap between attitudes and behavior. You are skeptical of large claimed effects.

Reference points for calibration:
- In comparable megastudies, average effects of single text messages on 0-100 attitude
  sliders are small: |ATE| typically 0-3 points, most often under 1 point.
- Effects of a single message exposure on real effortful behavior are typically near zero;
  low-cost in-survey actions (like agreeing to share a post) can move somewhat more.
- Proximal outcomes (beliefs directly targeted by the message) move more than distal
  ones (policy support, behavior).
- U.S. climate attitudes are strongly polarized; many liberals are near the scale ceiling,
  so headroom is concentrated among conservatives and moderates.
- A few messages backfire on some outcomes; the average message does not.

A preregistered online experiment (part of a 63-country 'intervention tournament') tested short interventions to stimulate climate action. This is the U.S. arm: 8,253 U.S. adults recruited online, ~670 per intervention arm and ~670 in control. Between-subjects design: each participant was randomly assigned to ONE intervention (or a neutral control text), then immediately completed the outcome measures. Belief and policy outcomes are 0-100 sliders.

CONTROL condition: participants read a neutral literary excerpt (from Dickens' Great Expectations) of similar length, reproduced below.

### Control_page1

### Control_distract
As soon as the great black velvet pall outside my little window was shot with grey, I got up and went downstairs; every board upon the way, and every crack in every board calling after me, "Stop thief!" and "Get up, Mrs. Joe!" In the pantry, which was far more abundantly supplied than usual, owing to the season, I was very much alarmed by a hare hanging up by the heels, whom I rather thought I caught, when my back was half turned, winking. I had no time for verification, no time for selection, no time for anything, for I had no time to spare. I stole some bread, some rind of cheese, about half a jar of mincemeat (which I tied up in my pocket-handkerchief with my last night’s slice), some brandy from a stone bottle (which I decanted into a glass bottle I had secretly used for making that intoxicating fluid, Spanish-liquorice-water, up in my room: diluting the stone bottle from a jug in the kitchen cupboard), a meat bone with very little on it, and a beautiful round compact pork pie. I was nearly going away without the pie, but I was tempted to mount upon a shelf, to look what it was that was put away so carefully in a covered earthenware dish in a corner, and I found it was the pie, and I took it in the hope that it was not intended for early use, and would not be missed for some time. 

 You will be able to advance the page shortly

In what follows, you will be shown a flyer and then you will be asked to answer a series of questions. 
 The flyer will be on the screen for 20 seconds, during which you are encouraged to read the information it displays. After 20 seconds you will be able to advance the page.

### identity_intro2
Imagine you are seeing this flyer in your neighborhood. Please read it carefully!  
 You will be able to advance the page in 20 seconds.

### identity_scale1
If you are taking steps towards reducing your carbon footprint, to what extent would you feel like
you are doing so together with other Americans?

### identity_scale2
To what extent do you feel like taking steps towards reducing your carbon footprint is something shared with other Americans?

### Identity_scale3
To what extent do you feel like taking steps towards reducing your carbon footprint involves a sense of togetherness with other Americans?

### identity_scale4
How common do you think it is for Americans to take steps towards reducing their carbon footprint?

### identity_scale5
How often do you think Americans make an effort towards reducing their carbon footprint?

### identity_scale6
How many Americans do you think make an effort towards reducing their carbon footprint?

### identity_scale7
How much do you
feel like other Americans think it is good to take steps towards reducing their carbon footprint?

### identity_scale8
How much do you
feel like other Americans think you should take steps towards reducing your carbon footprint?

### identity_scale9
How strongly do you identify with your fellow Americans?

### identity_scale10
How important is being American to your identity?

### identity_scale11
How important is being similar to other Americans to you?

### identity_scale12
How interested are you in reducing your carbon emissions?

### identity_scale13
To what degree do you support policies aimed at reducing greenhouse gasses?

### identity_scale14
To what degree would you share climate change information on social media?

### identity_scale15
How interested are you in donating to tree planting organizations?

OUTCOME MEASURES (all answered immediately post-treatment):

[wept] (predict ATE in pages completed on the 0-8 task scale)
Work for Environmental Protection Task (real effortful behavior): a voluntary, tedious number-identification task of up to 8 pages; each completed page triggers a real tree-planting donation. Participants can stop at any time. Outcome = number of pages completed (0-8; the control-group mean is roughly 5).

[policy] (predict ATE in points on the 0-100 slider scale)
Climate policy support: mean of 9 agreement sliders (0-100), 'I support...' raising carbon taxes on fossil fuels; expanding public transportation; more EV charging stations; more wind/solar energy; airline carbon taxes; protecting forests/land; green jobs investment; clean-waterways laws; taxes on carbon-intense foods.

[belief] (predict ATE in points on the 0-100 slider scale)
Belief in climate change: mean of 4 accuracy ratings (0-100 sliders) of the statements 'Human activities are causing climate change', 'Climate change poses a serious threat to humanity', 'Taking action to fight climate change is necessary to avoid a global catastrophe', 'Climate change is a global emergency'.

[share] (predict ATE in probability (proportion willing to share, 0-1 scale))
Willingness to share climate information on social media (yes/no): participants saw a short factual climate post (about cutting food-related emissions by eating less meat/dairy) and were asked 'Are you willing to share this information on your social media?'. Predict the ATE as a change in the proportion answering yes (the control-group proportion is roughly 0.5).

Task: for EACH outcome, predict the average treatment effect (ATE) of THIS intervention versus the pooled control group — intervention mean minus control mean — in the outcome's native units as specified above. Consider the mechanism of this specific message, its likely reception across the U.S. political spectrum, measurement reactivity, and how it compares to typical messages in such megastudies. Small and null effects are common; sign matters — give your best point estimate, not a hedge toward zero if you genuinely expect an effect.

Respond with ONLY a JSON object, no markdown fences, in exactly this form:
{"predictions": {"wept": <float>, "policy": <float>, "belief": <float>, "share": <float>}, "rationale": "<2-4 sentences>"}
